description: We turn lunar data into mission decisions. We're a 3-person İstanbul team: a lead working on edge AI and space data (papers at IEEE HPEC and IAC 2026), an electronics and software builder (PCB, C#, Python, C++), and a strategist handling storytelling and delivery. Roles are clear from hour one, so we ship a working demo, not just slides. Our focus is the Lunar Landing Site Navigator: showing not just where the Sun and Earth are, but whether a south-pole mission survives.
summary:
The next wave of Moon landings is aimed at the lunar south pole, where the Sun barely clears the horizon and the terrain can hide Earth. There, a few hundred metres and a few days decide whether a lander has power and can call home. In March 2025, Athena came to rest in a shadowed crater near the pole and lasted under 13 hours.

Most tools check a site you have already chosen. AdaptLab does the opposite. You say what the mission is for (a safe landing, water ice, Artemis…), and it searches 21,856 points across the south pole, every hour of every landing day. It uses NASA LOLA terrain, JPL ephemerides and the Deep Space Network schedule. It returns the best sites and dates, with success odds and the biggest risk named.

We replayed real landings: AdaptLab's sunlight matches Chandrayaan-3 (11.9 days modelled vs about 11 worked) and Blue Ghost 1 (14.5 vs about 14).
details: What it does 1. Choose the goal, the lander, the length of stay and the dates (Simple interface). Or set every requirement yourself (Advanced). 2. The search: 21,856 points on a 2 km grid around the south pole (or 41,276 across the whole Moon at about 30 km) × every landing day in the window × every hour of the stay. All of it runs in the browser in about a second. 3. For each point and date it checks: - sunlight: how much of the Sun's disc is above the real terrain horizon; - Earth in view, with a free DSN dish; - the longest darkness; - a battery model; - the slope of the landing zone from LOLA 40 m slopes; - the distance to ice-stable cold traps. 4. You get: - ranked sites and dates with GO/NO-GO; - success odds from hundreds of simulated missions, with the biggest risk named; - countdowns to sunset and Earth-set after touchdown; - a launch-slip strip ("slip 2 days → NO-GO, and why"); - a mission film from launch to touchdown; - a PDF report. - Any coordinate can also be checked directly (Advanced). Why it matters: it turns "is my site OK?" into "where and when should we go?", which is the question mission planners ask first. How we checked it: - Real landings replayed (Chandrayaan-3, Blue Ghost 1, SLIM, IM-1, Chang'e 6). The two upright landers match. The tilted ones show the model's limits, and we say so. - Fast horizons are within 0.5 points of full-resolution horizons (median, 27 sites). - Our slopes agree with LOLA's official 40 m slope map (r = 0.94, median 1.15°, 6,620 points). - The browser engine matches a Python reference implementation in automated tests. Limits (stated in the app): this is a planning and screening tool, not a landing certification. The 2 km polar grid can miss small ridges. The success odds are an estimate. Built with: TypeScript, React, three.js (react-three-fiber), Web Workers, Python (data preparation), Vercel. English and Turkish. Use of AI: the team used AI coding assistants (Anthropic Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, xAI Grok) to write and test code and to run visual QA. Every number shown comes from the engine and the data above, not from an AI model. In the app, the optional guide "Luna" answers questions with Google Gemini, using only the numbers the page sends it. Narration uses ElevenLabs text-to-speech. Before the hackathon: part of the engine existed before the event. The repository tag pre-hackathon (commit e616415) marks exactly what was built earlier. Everything after it was built during Space Apps 2026.
